transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-20
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morales (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood CSM); Samir Patel (Cartesio CTO), Lina Gomez (Eng Mgr), Maya Brooks (SRE)

Summary:
Quick weekly POC sync to review the last lab run comparing Redwood hosted config vs their baseline (CloudGenAI). Focus on latency/throughput tradeoffs and tuning batch/prefetch/kv cache. Agreed next steps to run larger concurrent microbench and share sanitized traces.

Topics:
- p95/p99 differences and tail behavior
- batching policy and max latency knobs
- KV cache prewarm and prefix cache effectiveness
- network egress and VPC middleware affecting tail latency
- validation plan for production-like traffic

Action items (short):
- Redwood to run scale microbench and share results
- Customer to share traffic trace
- Follow-up infra deep-dive sched

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll kick off, this is the week three poc sync for Cartesio. quick round of intros real quick.
[00:12] Samir: hey Samir here, CTO. thanks.
[00:15] Lina: Lina, engineering manager.
[00:18] Maya: Maya, SRE.
[00:20] Alex: cool, priya and diego from our side as well. uh objective today: review the lab runs you sent last night, go over p95/p99 gaps versus the baseline, and propose tuning changes.
[00:33] Priya: yeah i pulled the numbers, um i can share my screen after, but high-level: when we mirror the baseline config (CloudGenAI) we see similar p50 but our p95 is ~12% lower and p99 is around 18% lower at 256-token average for the chat flow. at higher concurrency the gap grows.
[00:50] Samir: when you say lower do you mean better? i'm sorry my english is...
[00:54] Priya: sorry yeah i mean our latency is lower = better. so p95 is lower.
[00:58] Lina: ok got it. we care mostly about p95 for interactive use, p99 for SLAs.
[01:05] Priya: notable caveat: the baseline run used an older model variant with smaller kv window but higher single-thread throughput, so the workload characteristics differ slightly.
[01:18] Maya: we also saw some outliers around 1800ms at peak, which coincide with OS-level context switches on the host, maybe network jitter.
[01:26] Alex: yeah this is where the VPC and egress path matters. our number for tail latency was stable when we put the test in the same AZ and disabled outbound firewall-as-a-service, which suggests some network hop in their infra.
[01:40] Samir: we are running through a third-party firewall that does DPI, could that add 200-300ms?
[01:46] Priya: definitely possible. DPI and SYN proxy can add non-trivial tail. worth validating with an in-AZ test.
[01:53] Lina: what about batching? our frontend currently sends short bursts of 1-3 requests which i think hurts batching efficiency.
[01:59] Priya: right, default continuous batching takes advantage of those bursts but when traffic is spiky it sometimes underfills batches. we recommended trying max_batch 8 with a max_latency_ms of 20, and also enabling prefix caching for repeated prompts.
[02:15] Samir: prefix cache? do you mean the KV cache we chatted about?
[02:17] Alex: yeah kv cache/prefix cache, sometimes the transcriber hears 'K V cash' which is funny. basically caching the key/value layers for repeated context windows so subsequent requests skip recompute.
[02:29] Maya: in our baseline they didn't use KV prewarm, that might explain the initial hit in latency for warm-up connections.
[02:34] Priya: our lab run with kv prewarm reduced p95 by ~9% under steady-state. we also tried quantization to int8 and that helped throughput but introduced a small BLEU-style delta in output — not a dealbreaker for your use case?
[02:50] Samir: for summarization flows we can tolerate small changes but not hallucinations. how did you measure quality?
[02:57] Priya: we used the eval harness you provided and the reference prompt set — token-level similarity and a small human spot check. quality delta was within threshold. we'll share the diffset.
[03:08] Lina: you mentioned dedicated vs hosted earlier, we are leaning hosted initially but may want dedicated later. does that change tuning?
[03:15] Alex: same API surface but dedicated gives you pinned GPU pools and you can set more aggressive batching and larger kv prewarm windows. hosted is fine for most workloads; dedicated reduces inter-tenant jitter.
[03:25] Maya: cost-wise how big is the delta?
[03:28] Alex: depends on commit size. dedicated is a committed monthly price vs hosted per-token; we can run a cost simulation after we finalize throughput numbers.
[03:36] Samir: back to results: how reproducible are these runs? we saw variance between runs.
[03:41] Priya: variance usually comes from three places: traffic shape, network path, and model kernel placement. we instrumented GPU utilization and saw some host-side context where the scheduler migrated processes, causing tail spikes.
[03:55] Lina: is that a kube autoscaler thing?
[03:58] Priya: possibly — in the lab we pinned cores to reduce interference, in production kube scheduler can cause noisy neighbors. dedicated removes most of that.
[04:07] Alex: quick note: we also validated with a 99th-percentile token rate and observed that continuous batching's dynamic windowing improved throughput by 17% vs fixed batch. for interactive p95 we still recommend conservative max_latency to avoid perceived slowness.
[04:22] Samir: ok can you walk through the proposed microbench we asked for?
[04:26] Priya: sure. plan: 1) run grpc-based microbench at 2k/5k/10k concurrent virtual users with representative token distribution, 2) compare three configs: baseline (CloudGen-like), Redwood-hosted default, Redwood-hosted tuned (max_batch 8, max_latency_ms 20, kv prewarm), 3) collect p50/p95/p99, cpu/gpu counters, network RTT histograms, and kernel-level traces where possible.
[04:48] Maya: how long for each run?
[04:50] Priya: make each run 15 minutes steady-state; include a 5-minute warm-up. that should fit into your window.
[04:57] Alex: we'll also add a single-AZ no-egress variant to isolate the firewall effects you mentioned.
[05:04] Samir: perfect. about the baseline provider config: do you need exact instance types?
[05:09] Priya: yes, that helps. if you can share the CloudGen instance type, concurrency limits, and any autoscale settings, we will mirror it as closely as possible.
[05:18] Lina: we'll pull that from our procurement notes and send over.
[05:22] Maya: quick question about encryption and KMS: if we enable KV prewarm with dedicated, does that surface any key material on the host?
[05:30] Alex: no, keys stay in the KMS and we use envelope encryption; the runtime only has derived ephemeral keys. for private deployments the customer can bring their own HSM.
[05:39] Samir: we need SOC2 artifacts and audit logs for the POC review.
[05:43] Diego: we'll send the SOC 2 summary, SSO/SAML doc, and an example audit trail extract.
[05:50] Priya: last thing — we noticed the baseline had a slightly different tokenization which impacted token counts; you might be overestimating tokens sent per request. could you confirm the tokenizer version?
[06:00] Samir: good catch, i'll check the tokenizer and send version.
[06:05] Alex: to recap next steps: Redwood runs scale microbench, customer shares trace + baseline config, both sides review results and then schedule infra deep-dive.
[06:15] Lina: sounds good.
[06:17] Maya: thanks.
[06:19] Alex: alright thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and a calendar invite for the deep-dive.
[06:25] Samir: thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
